question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Quotient of Complex Numbers in Polar Form
question.problem: Express $z=\frac{5}{4+3\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give $\theta $ in radians to three decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $4-3\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{5}{4+3\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{5(4-3\text{i})}{(4+3\text{i})(4-3\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{5(4-3\text{i})}{{4}^{2}-9{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5(4-3\text{i})}{16+9} \\  & =\frac{5(4-3\text{i})}{25} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}-\frac{3}{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{4}{5}-\frac{3}{5}\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2}+{(-\frac{3}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{25}+\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16+9}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $ represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\frac{4}{5}$ is positive and $y=-\frac{3}{5}$ is negative, $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{(-\frac{3}{5})}{(\frac{4}{5})}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) \\  & ≈5.640,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5.640)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5.640)
$$
